title: Computer System Architecture (Memory and I/O)
learningGoals: Explain locality of reference (spatial and temporal), the 80/20 rule, and how it shapes code (loop order, row-major arrays).
Compare SRAM vs DRAM, RAM vs ROM, and say where each sits in the hierarchy.
Explain primary vs secondary memory, memory-mapped I/O, buffer cache and swap space.
Compare block vs character devices with the 1024-byte example.
Compare HDD vs SSD, and NAND vs NOR flash, including erase-before-write and wear levelling.
Classify common I/O devices and explain why I/O is a privileged (kernel-mode) operation.
sirStressed: "Programs run faster when data stays close to the CPU." Data always moves closer to the CPU, and waiting time is the sum of the movement costs.
A faster CPU ≠ a faster program. Memory, I/O, locality and coordination set the limit.
The memory hierarchy exists because no single memory technology is best at everything.
The memory-access simulation activity: repeated data gets faster (a hit), and far-away data adds waiting (a miss). "It's about thinking like the computer."
TA: in modern CPUs, L2 is usually private per core and L3 is shared. The processor keeps frequently used data in cache, and the cache exploits locality.
TA: spatial locality is a hardware/memory idea, not the same as a database index.
TA (exam question in chat): "Is the examination theory based subjective or objective?", answered "Subjective". Be ready to explain in words, not just pick options.
commonTraps: Swapping spatial and temporal locality (the most common quiz mistake).
Saying DRAM is used for cache. Cache = SRAM; main memory = DRAM.
Forgetting that DRAM needs refresh because of its capacitor.
Thinking an SSD has seek time. It doesn't: access time is constant.
Thinking an SSD can overwrite a block in place. It needs an erase first, and wear levelling spreads the writes.
Mixing up NAND (storage, cheap, dense) with NOR (execute-in-place, firmware, bit-level writes).
Thinking user programs can read devices directly. All I/O is privileged, through the kernel.
Saying "random access" means random speed. It means the same access time for every location.
summary: CPU computes or waits. Hierarchy analogy: desk (cache) / bookshelf (RAM) / storeroom (disk).
80/20 rule (loops). Temporal = reuse the same data soon. Spatial = use neighbouring data next. Transfers are blocks so later accesses hit.
Row-major arrays: loop i outside and j inside. Swapping them causes misses.
SRAM (transistors, no refresh, fast, hardware-controlled) is cache. DRAM (capacitor, refresh, slower, OS-controlled) is main memory. ROM: e.g. Mask ROM, written at manufacture.
Register (flip-flops) > cache (SRAM) > RAM (DRAM) in speed and cost per byte.
Byte < word < block (cache line). For example, 64-byte line / 8-byte word = 8 words.
Secondary memory is persistent. A miss there causes a context switch. Buffer cache / memory-mapped I/O: only the first byte of a block is real I/O. Swap space = virtual memory.
Character vs block: 1024 I/Os vs 1 I/O for 1024 bytes.
HDD: access = seek + rotational latency + transfer. SSD: constant access, reads ≫ writes, erase-before-write, wear levelling, accumulated writes.
Devices: input, output, or both. All I/O is privileged, through the OS.

questions.prompt: Which statement is TRUE with respect to spatial locality?

options.text: Use data stored adjacent to the last accessed data
Reuse the same data within a short time
Access memory in strictly increasing order

questions.explanation: spatial = neighbouring addresses are likely next.

questions.prompt: Which statement is TRUE with respect to temporal locality? (options as above, D = access sequentially)

options.text: Use data stored adjacent to the last accessed data
Reuse the same data within a short time

questions.explanation: temporal = the same data is reused soon. (Your earlier attempt picked A, which is spatial. Don't swap them!)

questions.prompt: In spatial locality, when one memory location is accessed, it's likely that:

options.text: The same location will be accessed soon
Nearby locations will be accessed soon

questions.explanation: nearby locations, which is the definition of spatial locality. Option A describes temporal locality.

questions.prompt: Cache memory systems exploit spatial locality by:

options.text: Storing only the most frequently accessed variable
Fetching an entire block of contiguous memory, not just one word

questions.explanation: bringing in a whole block means the neighbouring words are already in the cache when you need them.

questions.prompt: The most recently accessed data is kept in registers to:
questions.explanation: recently used data is likely to be reused soon, so it's kept closest to the CPU.

questions.prompt: For this code, which variable has the highest temporal locality and which has the least?

options.text: An element of A highest, j least
i highest, an element of A least
An element of A highest, A[0] least

questions.explanation: i is used on every iteration (the condition, the increment and the indexes). j is declared but never used, so it has zero reuse.

questions.prompt: The most recently accessed block is kept in the L1 cache to:
questions.explanation: a block helps spatial locality (its neighbours come along), and keeping it recent helps temporal locality (reuse).
topicTags: Importance of Locality of Reference in Programming

questions.prompt: For the same Fibonacci-array code, which variable has the highest temporal and which has the highest spatial locality?

options.text: i highest temporal, array A highest spatial
An element of A highest temporal, i highest spatial
i highest temporal, an element of A highest spatial
An element of A highest temporal, A[0] highest spatial

questions.explanation: spatial locality is a property of the whole array walked in sequence, not of a single element. i is reused every iteration.
topicTags: Importance of Locality of Reference in Programming

questions.prompt: Which option best suits semiconductor memories?

options.text: They take constant time to access data irrespective of location

questions.explanation: RAM is "random access", so every location takes the same time (unlike a disk). Option D is wrong because ROM is read-only.
topicTags: Introduction to Primary Memory: RAM and ROM

questions.prompt: Which statement is FALSE regarding RAM access time?

options.text: Smaller RAM has less access time
RAM closer to the processor is faster

questions.explanation: SRAM (the cache) is faster than DRAM (main memory), so D is the false statement.
topicTags: Introduction to Primary Memory: RAM and ROM

questions.prompt: (i) SRAMs are transparent to the OS. (ii) One SRAM bit takes less space than one DRAM bit.
questions.explanation: caches (SRAM) are hardware-managed and invisible to the OS. An SRAM cell uses about 6 transistors, so it's bigger than a DRAM cell (1 transistor + 1 capacitor).

questions.prompt: (i) SRAMs follow the inclusive property. (ii) L3 has an equal or bigger block size than L2.
questions.explanation: L1 ⊂ L2 ⊂ L3 (inclusive), and block sizes grow as you go down the hierarchy.

questions.prompt: (i) DRAMs are transparent to the OS. (ii) One DRAM bit takes less space than one SRAM bit.
questions.explanation: main memory (DRAM) is managed by the OS (paging, allocation), so it isn't transparent. A DRAM cell (1T + 1C) is smaller than an SRAM cell. worked out, not from the quiz review.

questions.prompt: (i) DRAM needs refreshing at regular intervals to keep its data. (ii) DRAM has an equal or bigger block size than L2.
questions.explanation: the capacitors leak, so they need refreshing. The block (page) size grows as you go lower in the hierarchy. worked out, not from the quiz review.

questions.prompt: Dual-mode protection is for protecting ______.
questions.explanation: I/O instructions are privileged and run only in kernel mode, so user programs must go through the OS.
topicTags: Introduction to Secondary Memory and I/O Devices

questions.prompt: Which one is persistent data storage?
questions.explanation: only secondary storage keeps its data without power.
topicTags: Introduction to Secondary Memory and I/O Devices

questions.prompt: How can block-device performance be improved? (The quiz marked two answers)

options.text: Converting block access to character access

questions.explanation: the buffer cache keeps a whole block in memory, so later byte reads are served from RAM. In effect, block access is converted into fast character-style access (only the first byte costs a real I/O).

questions.prompt: Block devices require ______ to be handled in main memory to improve performance.
questions.explanation: "buffer cache" is the lecture's term.

questions.prompt: (i) Zoned hard disks have a higher capacity than conventional ones. (ii) Within a zone, the outermost track has more sectors than the innermost track of that zone.
questions.explanation: zoning packs more sectors onto the outer zones, which raises capacity. But within one zone every track has the same number of sectors, so (ii) is false.

questions.prompt: A raw ("row") partition is used by the OS for ______. (The quiz marked two answers)
questions.explanation: a raw partition has no file system. It's used for swap space (virtual memory) and the boot loader area.

questions.prompt: The main drawback of SSDs compared with a hard disk is:
questions.explanation: flash blocks survive only a limited number of erase/write cycles, which is why wear levelling exists.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT an advantage of SSDs?
questions.explanation: writes are slow (erase-before-write), so reads ≫ writes.

questions.prompt: Which characteristic suits NOR flash?
questions.explanation: NOR is reliable, byte-addressable and execute-in-place (firmware), so it needs no ECC. It's costly and low-capacity, with slow writes.
topicTags: SSD as Primary Memory vs Secondary Memory

questions.prompt: Which characteristic suits NAND flash?
questions.explanation: NAND = high density, cheap, used for bulk SSD storage.
topicTags: SSD as Primary Memory vs Secondary Memory

questions.prompt: Which is NOT an input-output (both ways) device?
questions.explanation: a printer is output-only. The others both read and write.

questions.prompt: Which one is an input-output device?
questions.explanation: a touch screen displays (output) and senses touch (input). A scanner and a joystick are input only, and a speaker is output only. Note: a second partial "Locality of Reference" capture (from your own earlier attempt) duplicates Q2 of the first quiz above, so it isn't repeated.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes temporal locality?

options.text: Using data stored next to the last accessed data
Reusing the same data within a short time

questions.explanation: Reusing the same data soon is temporal. (a) describes spatial locality.

questions.prompt: L1, L2 and L3 caches are typically built from:
questions.explanation: SRAM: fast, transistor-based, no refresh.

questions.prompt: Which memory needs periodic refreshing?
questions.explanation: DRAM. Its capacitor leaks charge.

questions.prompt: Reading 1024 bytes from a keyboard versus from a disk file (block size ≥ 1024 bytes) needs how many I/O operations respectively?
questions.explanation: A character device needs one I/O per byte (1024 mode switches). A block device needs one I/O, and the rest come from the buffer cache.

questions.prompt: Which flash type supports execute-in-place and is used mainly for firmware/ROM?
questions.explanation: NOR flash: bit-level writes, fast reads, execute-in-place.

questions.prompt: The SSD technique that spreads writes evenly across blocks is:
questions.explanation: Wear levelling keeps the write counts even so no part wears out early.

questions.prompt: Why does swapping the loops ( j outer, i inner) when filling A[1024] [1024] in C slow the program down?
correctAnswers: C arrays are row-major. With i inside, each access jumps a whole row (1024 elements), landing in a different block every time. That destroys spatial locality and causes many cache misses.
questions.explanation: C arrays are row-major. With i inside, each access jumps a whole row (1024 elements), landing in a different block every time. That destroys spatial locality and causes many cache misses.

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why we don't build all memory from SRAM.
correctAnswers: SRAM is too expensive per GB and too power-hungry. Its density is too low for gigabytes. (The hierarchy exists because no single technology wins everywhere.)
questions.explanation: SRAM is too expensive per GB and too power-hungry. Its density is too low for gigabytes. (The hierarchy exists because no single technology wins everywhere.)

questions.prompt: A disk spins at 6000 RPM. Find the average rotational latency.
correctAnswers: One rotation takes 60/6000 s = 10 ms. The average latency is half a rotation, 5 ms.
questions.explanation: One rotation takes 60/6000 s = 10 ms. The average latency is half a rotation, 5 ms.

questions.prompt: Why must every I/O access go through the operating system?
correctAnswers: I/O instructions are privileged (dual-mode protection). Only the kernel can run them, which protects devices and data from misuse. User programs make requests through the OS.
questions.explanation: I/O instructions are privileged (dual-mode protection). Only the kernel can run them, which protects devices and data from misuse. User programs make requests through the OS.
